entries.be598d1db4b25105d41bcafd5eb4bbc735bf3281: <div eID="gen24038" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen24039" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24040" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24040" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24039" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24041" type="x-p"/> Wisdom builds her house, makes her provision for a great feast, calls her guests, and exhorts them to partake of her entertainment, <reference osisRef="Pro.9.1-Pro.9.6">Pro 9:1-6</reference>. Different admonitions relative to the acquisition of wisdom, <reference osisRef="Pro.9.7-Pro.9.12">Pro 9:7-12</reference>. The character and conduct of a bad woman, <reference osisRef="Pro.9.13-Pro.9.18">Pro 9:13-18</reference>. <div eID="gen24041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24042" type="x-p"/> The same Wisdom speaks here who spoke in the preceding chapter. There she represented herself as manifest in all the works of God in the natural world; all being constructed according to counsels proceeding from an infinite understanding. Here, she represents herself as the great potentate, who was to rule all that she had constructed, and having an immense family to provide for, had made an abundant provision, and calls all to partake of it. This, says Calmet, is the continuation of the parable begun in the preceding chapter, where wisdom is represented as a venerable lady, whose real beauties and solid promises are opposed to the false allurements of Pleasure, who was represented in the seventh chapter under the idea of a debauched and impudent woman. This one, to draw young people into her snares, describes the perfumes, the bed, and the festival which she has prepared. Wisdom acts in the same way: but, instead of the debauchery, the false pleasures, and the criminal connections which pleasure had promised, offers her guests a strong, well-built, magnificent palace, chaste and solid pleasures, salutary instructions, and a life crowned with blessedness. This is the sum and the substance of the parable; but as in the preceding part, so in this, men have produced strange creatures of their own brain by way of explanation. One specimen of this mode of interpretation may suffice. <div eID="gen24042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24043" type="x-p"/> The house built by wisdom is the holy humanity of Jesus Christ; the seven pillars are the seven sacraments, or the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost, or the whole of the apostles, preachers, and ministers of the Church; the slain beasts are the sacrifice of Christ's body upon the cross; and the bread and mingled wine are the bread and wine in the sacrament of the Lord's Supper! - Fathers and Doctors. <div eID="gen24043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24044" type="x-p"/> If we have recourse to any other particulars than those given above in the summary of the chapter, let us follow the first part of the parable, where wisdom is represented as laying the plan of the creation; and then perhaps we may say with safety, that wisdom, having produced the grand ichnopraph or ground plot of the whole, with all the requisite elevations and specifications of materials, comes to show us, in this part, that the whole has been constructed on this plan; and specifies the end for which this august building has been raised. <div eID="gen24044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24045" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen24045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24046" type="x-p"/> Wisdom hath builded her house - The eternal counsel of God has framed the universe. <div eID="gen24046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24047" type="x-p"/> She hath hewn out her seven pillars - Every thing has been so constructed as to exhibit a scene of grandeur, stability, and durableness.
entries.199a62edc725ad9de389e33e6323bf5598beb5f5: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen24047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24048" type="x-p"/> She hath killed her beasts - God has made the most ample provision for the innumerable tribes of animal and intellectual beings, which people the whole vortex of created nature.
entries.aa7588ecdd0da167fb1f5cf3186e4301b7038322: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen24048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24049" type="x-p"/> She hath sent forth her maidens - The wisdom of God has made use of the most proper means to communicate Divine knowledge to the inhabitants of the earth; as a good and gracious Creator wills to teach them whence they came, how they are supported, whither they are going, and for what end they were formed. It is a custom to the present day, in Asiatic countries, to send their invitations to guests by a company of females, preceded by eunuchs: they go to the doors of the invited, and deliver their message.
entries.c50596ffab1f54093aa4348649e187181fcf98c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen24049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24050" type="x-p"/> Whoso is simple - Let the young, heedless, and giddy attend to my teaching. <div eID="gen24050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24051" type="x-p"/> Him that wanteth understanding - Literally, he that wanteth a heart; who is without couraye, is feeble and fickle, and easily drawn aside from the holy commandment.
entries.c1c2b1c027a55ea3528420d1dd6a3a780bfc1a45: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen24051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24052" type="x-p"/> Come, eat of my bread - Not only receive my instructions, but act according to my directions. <div eID="gen24052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24053" type="x-p"/> Drink of the wine - I have mingled - Enter into my counsels; be not contented with superficial knowledge on any subject, where any thing deeper may be attained. Go by the streams to the fountain head. Look into the principles on which they were formed; investigate their nature, examine their properties, acquaint thyself with their relations, connections, influences, and various uses. See the skill power, and goodness of God in their creation. And when thou hast learned all within thy reach, know that thou knowest but little of the manifold wisdom of God. Let what thou hast learned humble thee, by showing thee how very little thou dost know. Thou hast drunk of the provided wine; but that wine was mingled with water, for God will hide pride from man. He dwells only on the surface of religious and philosophical learning, who does not perceive and feel that he is yet but a child in knowledge; that he see through a glass darkly; that he perceives men like trees walking; and that there are lengths, breadths, depths, and heights, in the works and ways of God, which it will require an eternity to fathom. Here below the pure wine is mingled with water: but this is God's work. Yet there is enough; do not therefore be contented with a little. To this subject the words of the poet may be well applied: - <div eID="gen24053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24054" type="x-p"/> A little learning is a dangerous thing; Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring: <div eID="gen24054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24055" type="x-p"/> For scanty draughts intoxicate the brain, <div eID="gen24055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24056" type="x-p"/> But drinking largely sobers us again. <div eID="gen24056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24057" type="x-p"/> Pope <div eID="gen24057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24058" type="x-p"/> Among the ancient Jews, Greek, and Romans, wine was rarely drank without being mingled with water; and among ancient writers we find several ordinances for this. Some direct three parts of water to one of wine; some five parts; and Pliny mentions some wines that required twenty waters: but the most common proportions appear to have been three parts of water to two of wine. But probably the יין מסך yayin masach, mingled wine, was wine mingled, not with water, to make it weaker; but with spices and other ingredients to make it stronger. The ingredients were honey, myrrh, mandragora, opium, and such like, which gave it not only an intoxicating but stupifying quality also. Perhaps the mixed wine here may mean wine of the strongest and best quality, that which was good to cheer and refresh the heart of man. <div eID="gen24058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24059" type="x-p"/> If we consider the mixed wine as meaning this strong wine, then the import of the metaphor will be, a thorough investigation of the works of God will invigorate the soul, strengthen all the mental powers, enlarge their capacity, and enable the mind to take the most exalted views of the wonders of God's skill manifested in the operations of his hand.
entries.1c7596e01b16d4f8c169e83f7c75ca6c813dfdef: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen24059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24060" type="x-p"/> Forsake the foolish - For the companion of fools must be a fool. <div eID="gen24060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24061" type="x-p"/> And live - Answer the end for which thou wert born.
entries.a58ac7db6e67705097545b832f76867d192ef07d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen24061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24062" type="x-p"/> He that reproveth a scorner - לץ lets, the person who mocks at sacred things; the libertine, the infidel; who turns the most serious things into ridicule, and, by his wit, often succeeds in rendering the person who reproves him ridiculous. Wisdom seems here to intimate that it is vain to attempt by reproof to amend such: and yet we must not suffer sin upon our neighbor; at all hazards, we must deliver our own soul. But no reproof should be given to any, but in the spirit of love and deep concern; and when they contradict and blaspheme, leave them to God.
entries.023f303ac3051013577e2143674ba94699714df6: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen24062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24063" type="x-p"/> Give instruction to a wise man - Literally give to the wise, and he will be wise. Whatever you give to such, they reap profit from it. They are like the bee, they extract honey from every flower.
entries.020600ff1c118cf79da59162d2dcfbf3fb8eb413: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen24063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24064" type="x-p"/> The fear of the Lord - See on <reference osisRef="Pro.1.7">Pro 1:7</reference> (note). The knowledge of the holy; קדשים kedoshim, of the holy ones: Sanctorum, of the saints - Vulgate. boulh agiwn, the counsel of the holy persons.
entries.b8c20d3aed97ca14bd516a759633c52d93498545: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen24064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24065" type="x-p"/> For by me thy days shall be multiplied - Vice shortens human life, by a necessity of consequence: and by the same, righteousness lengthens it. There is a long addition here in the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate: "He who trusts in falsity feeds on the winds; and is like him who chases the fowls of heaven. He forsakes the way of his own vineyard, and errs from the paths of his own inheritance. He enters also into lonely and desert places, and into a land abandoned to thirst; and his hands collect that which yieldeth no fruit."
entries.5acb4c36120aacc0233e9559db6659dde60a7253: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen24065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24066" type="x-p"/> If thou be wise - It is thy own interest to be religious. Though thy example may be very useful to thy neighbors and friends, yet the chief benefit is to thyself. But if thou scorn - refuse to receive - the doctrines of wisdom, and die in thy sins, thou alone shalt suffer the vengeance of an offended God.
entries.3f4aaee3e5d0755fbc4f8c1cdd50c3ec7f3566d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen24066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24067" type="x-p"/> A foolish woman is clamorous - Vain, empty women, are those that make most noise. And she that is full of clamor, has generally little or no sense. We have had this character already, see <reference osisRef="Pro.7.11">Pro 7:11</reference>. The translation of the Septuagint is very remarkable: Γυνη αφρων και θρασεια, ενδεης ψωμου γινεται, "A lewd and foolish woman shall be in need of a morsel of bread."
entries.572293b7bb660ea29f4a3b0aca5b2ca34f8618b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen24067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24068" type="x-p"/> For she sitteth at the door of her house - Her conduct here marks at once her folly, impudence, and poverty. See above on <reference osisRef="Pro.7.6">Pro 7:6</reference> (note), etc., where the reader will find a similar character.
entries.29cf828dc447adb1765d3e6a043f7de226e746b1: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen24068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24069" type="x-p"/> Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither - Folly or pleasure here personified, uses the very same expressions as employed by Wisdom, <reference osisRef="Pro.9.4">Pro 9:4</reference>. Wisdom says, "Let the simple turn in to me." No, says Folly, "Let the simple turn in to me." If he turn in to Wisdom, his folly shall be taken away and he shall become wise; if he turn in to Foliy, his darkness will be thickened, and his folly will remain. <div eID="gen24069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24070" type="x-p"/> Wisdom sets up her school to instruct the ignorant: <div eID="gen24070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24071" type="x-p"/> Folly sets her school up next door, to defeat the designs of Wisdom. <div eID="gen24071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24072" type="x-p"/> Thus the saying of the satirist appears to be verified: - "Wherever God erects a house of prayer, <div eID="gen24072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24073" type="x-p"/> The devil surely builds a chapel there. <div eID="gen24073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24074" type="x-p"/> And it is found upon examination, <div eID="gen24074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24075" type="x-p"/> The latter has the larger congregation." <div eID="gen24075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24076" type="x-p"/> De Foe.
entries.ead0b58e5af2edb36075583cbe737df5e9b7dc9b: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen24076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24077" type="x-p"/> Stolen waters are sweet - I suppose this to be a proverbial mode of expression, importing that illicit pleasures are sweeter than those which are legal The meaning is easy to be discerned; and the conduct of multitudes shows that they are ruled by this adage. On it are built all the adulterous intercourses in the land.
entries.a4bab0e07bfccf012fdbfb387de050f6d8aa2661: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen24077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24078" type="x-p"/> But he knoweth not that the dead are there - See on <reference osisRef="Pro.2.18">Pro 2:18</reference> (note). He does not know that it was in this way the first apostates from God and truth walked. רפאים rephaim; gigantev, the Giants - Septuagint. The sons of men, the earth-born, to distinguish them from the sons of God, those who were born from above. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Gen.6.1">Gen 6:1</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen24078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24079" type="x-p"/> Her guests are in the depths of hell - Those who have been drawn out of the way of understanding by profligacy have in general lost their lives, if not their souls, by their folly. The Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic make a long addition to this verse: "But draw thou back, that thou mayest not die in this place; neither fix thy eyes upon her; so shalt thou pass by those strange waters. But abstain thou from strange waters, and drink not of another's fountain, that thou mayest live a long time, and that years may be added to thy life." Of this addition there is nothing in the Hebrew, the Chaldee, or the Vulgate, as now printed: but in the editio princeps are the following words: Qui enim applicabitur illi descendet ad inferos; nam qui abscesserit ab ea salvabitur. These words were in the copy from which my old MS. Bible has been made, as the following version proves: Who forsoth schal ben joyned to hir, schal falle doun on to hell: for whi he that goth awai fro hir, schal be saved. Three of my own MSS. have the same reading.  <chapter eID="Prov.9"/> <div eID="gen24079" type="x-p"/>

entries.6be230d02b1a33d183404ea34dcaf63669cac695: <reference osisRef="Prov.9.1">Pro 9:1</reference> <div eID="gen10846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10847" type="x-p"/> Regarding חכמות, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 1:20. It is a <hi type="italic">plur. excellentiae</hi>, which is a variety of the <hi type="italic">plur. extensivus</hi>. Because it is the expression of a plural unity, it stands connected (as for the most part also אלהים, <hi type="italic">Deus</hi>) with the sing. of the predicate. The perfects enumerate all that Wisdom has done to prepare for her invitation. If we had a parable before us, the perf. would have run into the historical ותּשׁלח; but it is, as the תקרא shows, an allegorical picture of the arrangement and carrying out of a present reality. Instead of בּנתה לּהּ בּית there is בּנתה בּיתהּ, for the house is already in its origin represented as hers, and 1b is to be translated: she has hewn out her seven pillars (Hitzig); more correctly: her pillars, viz., seven (after the scheme דבּתם רעה, <reference osisRef="Gen.37.2">Gen 37:2</reference>); but the construction is closer. שׁבעה is, altogether like <reference osisRef="Exod.25.37">Exo 25:37</reference>, the accusative of the second object, or of the predicate after the species of <hi type="italic">verba</hi>, with the idea: to make something, turn into something, which take to themselves a double accusative, Gesen. §139, 2: <hi type="italic">excidit columnas suas ita ut septem essent</hi>. Since the figure is allegorical, we may not dispense with the interpretation of the number seven by the remark, “No emphasis lies in the number” (Bertheau). First, we must contemplate architecturally the house with seven pillars: “They are,” as Hitzig rightly remarks, “the pillars of the מסדּרון (porch) [<hi type="italic">vid</hi>. Bachmann under Jdg 3:23, and Wetstein under <reference osisRef="Ps.144.12">Psa 144:12</reference>, where חטב is used of the cutting out and hewing of wood, as חצב of the cutting out and hewing of stone] in the inner court, which bore up the gallery of the first (and second) floors: four of these in the corners and three in the middle of three sides; through the midst of these the way led into the court of the house-floor the area.” But we cannot agree with Hitzig in maintaining that, with the seven pillars of chap. 8 and 9, the author looks back to the first seven chapters (Arab. âbwab, gates) of this book; we think otherwise of the component members of this Introduction to the Book of Proverbs; and to call the sections of a book “gates, שׁערים,” is a late Arabico-Jewish custom, of which there is found no trace whatever in the O.T. To regard them also, with Heidenheim (cf. Dante’s Prose Writings, translated by Streckfuss, p. 77), as representing the seven liberal arts (שׁבע חכמות) is impracticable; for this division of the <hi type="italic">artes liberales</hi> into seven, consisting of the <hi type="italic">Trivium</hi> (Grammar, Rhetoric, and Dialectics) and <hi type="italic">Quadrivium</hi> (Music, Arithmetic, Geometry, and Astronomy), is not to be looked for within the old Israelitish territory, and besides, these were the sciences of this world which were so divided; but wisdom, to which the discourse here refers, is wholly a religious-moral subject. The Midrash thinks of the seven heavens (שׁבעה רקיעים), or the seven climates or parts of the earth (שׁבעה ארצות), as represented by them; but both references require artificial combinations, and have, as also the reference to the seven church-eras (Vitringa and Chr. Ben. Michaelis), this against them, that they are rendered probable neither from these introductory proverbial discourses, nor generally from the O.T. writings. The patristic and middle-age reference to the seven sacraments of the church passes sentence against itself; but the old interpretation is on the right path, when it suggests that the seven pillars are the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost. The seven-foldness of the manifestation of the Spirit, already brought near by the seven lamps of the sacred candelabra (the מנורה), is established by <reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Isa 11:2</reference> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">l.c</hi>.); and that Wisdom is the possessor and dispenser of the Spirit she herself testifies, Pro 1:23. Her Spirit is the “Spirit of wisdom;” but at the same time, since, born of God, she is mediatrix between God and the world, also the “Spirit of Jahve,” He is the “spirit of understanding,” the “spirit of counsel,” and the “spirit of might” (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Isa 11:2</reference>); for she says, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.14">Pro 8:14</reference>, “Counsel is mine, and reflection; I am understanding, I have strength.” He is also the “spirit of knowledge,” and the “spirit of the fear of the Lord” (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Isa 11:2</reference>); for fear and the knowledge of Jahve are, according to <reference osisRef="Prov.9.14">Pro 9:14</reference>, the beginning of wisdom, and essentially wisdom itself.
entries.f2138a8a27e95ffcdd319590ce71d2d91362d200: <reference osisRef="Prov.9.2">Pro 9:2</reference> <div eID="gen10847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10848" type="x-p"/> If thus the house of Wisdom is the place of her fellowship with those who honour her, the system of arrangements made by her, so as to disclose and communicate to her disciples the fulness of her strength and her gifts, then it is appropriate to understand by the seven pillars the seven virtues of her nature communicating themselves (apocalyptically expressed, the ἑπτὰ πνεύματα), which bear up and adorn the dwelling which she establishes among men. Flesh and wine are figures of the nourishment for the mind and the heart which is found with wisdom, and, without asking what the flesh and the wine specially mean, are figures of the manifold enjoyment which makes at once strong and happy. The segolate <hi type="italic">n. verbale</hi> טבח, which <reference osisRef="Prov.7.22">Pro 7:22</reference> denoted the slaughtering or the being slaughtered, signifies here, in the concrete sense, the slaughtered ox; Michaelis rightly remarks that טבח, in contradistinction to זבח, is the usual word for <hi type="italic">mactatio extrasacrificialis</hi>. Regarding מסך יין, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Isa.5.22">Isa 5:22</reference>; it is not meant of the mingling of wine with sweet scents and spices, but with water (warm or cold), and signifies simply to make the wine palatable (as κεραννύναι, <hi type="italic">temperare</hi>); the lxx ἐκέρασεν εἰς κρατῆρα, κρατήρ is the name of the vessel in which the mixing takes place; they drank not ἄκρατον, but κεκερασμένον ἄκρατον, Rev 14:10. The frequently occurring phrase ערך שׁלחן signifies to prepare the table (from שׁלּח, properly the unrolled and outspread leather cover), viz., by the placing out of the dishes (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding ערך, under <reference osisRef="Gen.22.9">Gen 22:9</reference>).
entries.1b6113d53538dcee553fb8c2a4c6311c2188d966: <reference osisRef="Prov.9.3">Pro 9:3</reference> <div eID="gen10848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10849" type="x-p"/> The verb קרא, when a feast is spoken of, means to invite; קראים, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.18">Pro 9:18</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.13">1Sa 9:13</reference>, etc.), are the guests. נערותיה the lxx translates τοὺς ἑαυτῆς δούλους, but certainly here the disciples are meant who already are in the service of Wisdom; but that those who are invited to Wisdom are thought of as feminine, arises from the tasteful execution of the picture. The invitation goes forth to be known to all far and wide, so that in her servants Wisdom takes her stand in the high places of the city. Instead of בּראשׁ, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.2">Pro 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.21">Pro 1:21</reference>, there is used here the expression על־גּפּי. We must distinguish the Semitic גּף (= ganf), wings, from גנף = כנף, to cover, and גּף (= gaff or ganf), the bark, which is derived either from גּפף or גּנף, Arab. jnf, <hi type="italic">convexus, incurvus et extrinsecus gibber fuit</hi>, hence originally any surface bent outwards or become crooked (cf. the roots cap, caf, קב כף גף גב, etc.), here the summit of a height (Fl.); thus not <hi type="italic">super alis</hi> (after the analogy of πτερύγιον, after Suidas = ἀκρωτήριον), but <hi type="italic">super dorsis</hi> (as in Lat. we say δορσυμ μοντις, and also <hi type="italic">viae</hi>).
entries.6a82a8f94d39d1a808dd3338c882ecd214548330: <reference osisRef="Prov.9.4-Prov.9.6">Pro 9:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen10849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10850" type="x-p"/> Now follows the street-sermon of Wisdom inviting to her banquet: 4 Who is simple? let him come hither!”    Whoso wanteth understanding, to him she saith: 5 “Come, eat of my bread,    And drink of the wine which I have mingled! 6 Cease, ye simple, and live,    And walk straight on in the way of understanding.” <div eID="gen10850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10851" type="x-p"/> The question מי פּתי (thus with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, not with <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>, it is to be written here and at <reference osisRef="Prov.9.16">Pro 9:16</reference>; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Baer’s <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 40), <hi type="italic">quis est imperitus</hi>, is, as <reference osisRef="Ps.25.12">Psa 25:12</reference>, only a more animated expression for <hi type="italic">quisquis est</hi>. The retiring into the background of the נערות (servants), and the immediate appearance of Wisdom herself, together with the interruption, as was to be expected, of her connected discourses by the אמרה לּו, are signs that the pure execution of the allegorical representation is her at an end. Hitzig seeks, by the rejection of <reference osisRef="Prov.9.4">Pro 9:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.5">Pro 9:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.7-Prov.9.10">Pro 9:7-10</reference>, to bring in a logical sequence; but these interpolations which he cuts out are yet far more inconceivable than the proverbial discourses in the mouth of Wisdom, abandoning the figure of a banquet, which besides are wholly in the spirit of the author of this book. That Folly invites to her, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.16">Pro 9:16</reference>, in the same words as are used by Wisdom, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.4">Pro 9:4</reference>, is not strange; both address themselves to the simple (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on פּתי at <reference osisRef="Prov.1.4">Pro 1:4</reference>) and those devoid of understanding (as the youth, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.7">Pro 7:7</reference>), and seek to bring to their side those who are accessible to evil as to good, and do not dully distinguish between them, which the emulating <hi type="italic">devertat huc</hi> of both imports. The fourth verse points partly backwards, and partly forwards; 4a has its introduction in the תקרא of <reference osisRef="Prov.9.3">Pro 9:3</reference>; on the contrary, 4b is itself the introduction of what follows. The setting forth of the <hi type="italic">nom. absolutus</hi> חסר־לב is conditioned by the form of 4a; the מי (cf. 4a) is continued (in 4b) without its needing to be supplied: <hi type="italic">excors</hi> (= <hi type="italic">si quis est excors</hi>) <hi type="italic">dicit ei</hi> (not <hi type="italic">dixit</hi>, because syntactically subordinating itself to the תקרא). It is a nominal clause, whose virtual predicate (the devoid of understanding is thus and thus addressed by her) as in Pro 9:16.
entries.d08e1c191f7f8dcdedc5e8e4fd199dd28ba3381b: <reference osisRef="Prov.9.7-Prov.9.9">Pro 9:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen10853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10854" type="x-p"/> In what now follows the discourse of Wisdom is continued; wherefore she directs her invitation to the simple, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, those who have not yet decided, and are perhaps susceptible of that which is better: 7 “He who correcteth a scorner draweth upon himself insult;    And he who communicateth instruction to a scorner, it is a dishonour to him. 8 Instruct not a scorner, lest he hate thee;    Give instruction to the wise, so he will love thee. 9 Give to the wise, and he becomes yet wiser;    Give knowledge to the upright, and he gains in knowledge.” <div eID="gen10854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10855" type="x-p"/> Zöckler thinks that herewith the reason for the summons to the “simple” to forsake the fellowship of men of their own sort, is assigned (he explains 6a as Ahron b. Joseph: הפרדו מן הפתאים); but his remark, that, under the term “simple,” mockers and wicked persons are comprehended as belonging to the same category, confounds two sharply distinguished classes of men. לץ is the freethinker who mocks at religion and virtue (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.1.22">Pro 1:22</reference>), and רשׁע the godless who shuns restraint by God and gives himself up to the unbridled impulse to evil. The course of thought in <reference osisRef="Prov.9.7">Pro 9:7</reference> and onwards shows why Wisdom, turning from the wise, who already are hers, directs herself only to the simple, and those who are devoid of understanding: she must pass over the לץ and רשׁע dna , because she can there hope for no receptivity for her invitation; she would, contrary to <reference osisRef="Matt.7.6">Mat 7:6</reference>, “give that which is holy to the dogs, and cast her pearls before swine.” יסר, παιδεύειν (with the prevailing idea of the bitter lesson of reproof and punishment), and הוכיח, ἐλέγχειν, are interchangeable conceptions, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.10">Psa 94:10</reference>; the ל is here exponent of the object (to bring an accusation against any one), as <reference osisRef="Prov.9.8">Pro 9:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.12">Pro 15:12</reference> (otherwise as <reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">Isa 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Isa 11:4</reference>, where it is the <hi type="italic">dat. commodi</hi>: to bring unrighteousness to light, in favour of the injured). יסר לץ is pointed with <hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi> of the penultima, and thus with the tone thrown back. The <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi>, placed in some editions between the two words, is masoretically inaccurate. He who reads the moral to the mocker brings disgrace to himself; the incorrigible replies to the goodwill with insult. Similar to the לקח לו here, is מרים <hi type="italic">tollit</hi> = <hi type="italic">reportat</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.25">Pro 3:25</reference>; Pro 4:27. In 7b מוּמו is by no means the object governed by וּמוכיח: and he who shows to the godless his fault (Meîri, Arama, Löwenstein: מומו = על־מומו, and thus also the <hi type="italic">Graec. Venet.</hi> μῶμον ἑαυτῷ, <hi type="italic">scil</hi>. λαμβάνει); plainly מומו is parallel with קלון. But מומו does not also subordinate itself to לקח as to the object. parallel קלון: <hi type="italic">maculam sibimet</hi> <hi type="italic">scil</hi>. <hi type="italic">acquirit</hi>; for, to be so understood, the author ought at least to have written לו מוּם. Much rather מומו is here, as at <reference osisRef="Deut.32.5">Deu 32:5</reference>, appos., thus pred. (Hitzig), without needing anything to be supplied: his blot it is, viz., this proceeding, which is equivalent to מוּמא הוּא ליהּ (Targ.), <hi type="italic">opprobrio ipsi est</hi>. Zöckler not incorrectly compares <reference osisRef="Ps.115.7">Psa 115:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.16">Ecc 5:16</reference>, but the expression (<hi type="italic">macula ejus</hi> = <hi type="italic">ipsi</hi>) lies here less remote from our form of expression. In other words: Whoever correcteth the mockers has only to expect hatred (אל־תוכח with the tone thrown back, according to rule; cf. on the contrary, Jdg 18:25), but on the other hand, love from the wise.
entries.02036e99ad27412c487813ff3b9e45787a0efcba: <reference osisRef="Prov.9.10">Pro 9:10</reference> <div eID="gen10857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10858" type="x-p"/> These words naturally follow: 10 “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of Jahve,      And the knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.” <div eID="gen10858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10859" type="x-p"/> This is the highest principle of the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi>, which stands (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.7">Pro 1:7</reference>) as a motto at the beginning of the Book of Proverbs. The lxx translate ראשׁית there (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.7">Pro 1:7</reference>), and תּחלּת here, by ἀρχή. Gusset distinguishes the two synonyms as <hi type="italic">pars optima</hi> and <hi type="italic">primus actus</hi>; but the former denotes the fear of God as that which stands in the uppermost place, to which all that Wisdom accomplishes subordinates itself; the latter as that which begins wisdom, that which it proposes to itself in its course. With יהוה is interchanged, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.5">Pro 2:5</reference>, אלהים, as here קדושׁים, as the internally multiplicative plur. (Dietrich, <hi type="italic">Abhandlungen</hi>, pp. 12, 45), as <reference osisRef="Prov.30.3">Pro 30:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.24.9">Jos 24:9</reference>; Hos 12:1, of God, the “Holy, holy, holy” (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.3">Isa 6:3</reference>), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, Him who is absolutely Holy. Michaelis inaccurately, following the ancients, who understood not this non-numerical plur.: <hi type="italic">cognitio quae sanctos facit et sanctis propria est</hi>. The דּעת, parallel with יראת, is meant of lively practical operative knowledge, which subordinates itself to this All-holy God as the normative but unapproachable pattern.
entries.fbc53b89a7605774a71a30f68d86d961093fe994: <reference osisRef="Prov.9.11">Pro 9:11</reference> <div eID="gen10859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10860" type="x-p"/> The singular reason for this proverb of Wisdom is now given: “For by me will thy days become many, <div eID="gen10860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10861" type="x-p"/> And the years of thy life will be increased.” <div eID="gen10861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10862" type="x-p"/> Incorrectly Hitzig: “and years of life will increase to thee;” הוסיף is always and everywhere (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, also <reference osisRef="Job.38.11">Job 38:11</reference>) transitive. In the similar passage, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.2">Pro 3:2</reference>, יוסיפו had as its subject the doctrine of Wisdom; here חכמה and בינה it is not practicable to interpret as subj., since 11a Wisdom is the subject discoursing - the expression follows the scheme, <hi type="italic">dicunt eos</hi> = <hi type="italic">dicuntur</hi>, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.7.3">Job 7:3</reference>; Gesen. §137 - a concealing of the operative cause, which lies near, where, as <reference osisRef="Prov.2.22">Pro 2:22</reference>, the discourse is of severe judgment, thus: they (viz., the heavenly Powers) will grant to thee years of life (חיּים in a pregnant sense, as <reference osisRef="Prov.3.2">Pro 3:2</reference>) in rich measure, so that constantly one span comes after another. But in what connection of consequence does this stand with the contents of the proverb, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.10">Pro 9:10</reference>? The ancients say that the clause with כי refers back to Pro 9:5. The <reference osisRef="Prov.9.7-Prov.9.10">Pro 9:7-10</reference> (according also to Fl.) are, as it were, parenthetic. Hitzig rejects these verses as an interpolation, but the connection of <reference osisRef="Prov.9.11">Pro 9:11</reference> with 5f. retains also something that is unsuitable: “steps forward on the way of knowledge, for by me shall thy days become many;” and if, as Hitzig supposes, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.12">Pro 9:12</reference> is undoubtedly genuine, whose connection with <reference osisRef="Prov.9.11">Pro 9:11</reference> is in no way obvious, then also will the difficulty of the connection of <reference osisRef="Prov.9.7-Prov.9.10">Pro 9:7-10</reference> with the preceding and the succeeding be no decisive mark of the want of genuineness of this course of thought. We have seen how the progress of <reference osisRef="Prov.9.6">Pro 9:6</reference> to 7 is mediated: the invitation of Wisdom goes forth to the receptive, with the exclusion of the irrecoverable. And <reference osisRef="Prov.9.11">Pro 9:11</reference> is related to <reference osisRef="Prov.9.10">Pro 9:10</reference>, as the proof of the cause from the effect. It is the fear of God with which Wisdom begins, the knowledge of God in which above all it consists, for by it is fulfilled the promise of life which is given to the fear of God, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.27">Pro 10:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.14.27">Pro 14:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.23">Pro 19:23</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.4.40">Deu 4:40</reference>, and to humility, which is bound up with it. Pro 10:17.
entries.1e2b3e185ad4e1ac87ca76a31075ffc4ff3adcba: <reference osisRef="Prov.9.12">Pro 9:12</reference> <div eID="gen10862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10863" type="x-p"/> This wisdom, resting on the fear of God, is itself a blessing to the wise: “If thou art wise, thou art wise for thyself; <div eID="gen10863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10864" type="x-p"/> And if thou mockest, thou alone shalt bear it.” <div eID="gen10864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10865" type="x-p"/> The lxx, with the Syr., mangle the thought of 12a, for they translate: if thou art wise for thyself, so also thou wilt be wise for thy neighbour. The <hi type="italic">dat. commodi</hi> לך means that it is for the personal advantage of the wise to be wise. The contrast expressed by Job 22:2.: not profitable to God, but to thyself (Hitzig), is scarcely intended, although, so far as the accentuation is antithetic, it is the nearest. The perf. ולצתּ is the hypothetical; Gesen. §126, 1. To bear anything, viz., anything sinful (חטא or עון), is equivalent to, to atone for it, <reference osisRef="Job.34.2">Job 34:2</reference>, cf. Num 9:13; Eze 23:35. Also 12b is a contrast scarcely aimed at. Wisdom is its own profit to man; libertinism is its own disgrace. Man decides, whenever he prefers to be wise, or to be a mocker of religion and of virtue, regarding his own weal and woe. With this <hi type="italic">nota bene</hi> the discourse of Wisdom closes.
entries.1e4573da41bea818e739786a36b9819762267609: <reference osisRef="Prov.9.13-Prov.9.15">Pro 9:13-15</reference> <div eID="gen10865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10866" type="x-p"/> The poet now brings before us another figure, for he personifies Folly working in opposition to Wisdom, and gives her a feminine name, as the contrast to Wisdom required, and thereby to indicate that the seduction, as the 13th proverbial discourse (chap. 7) has shown, appears especially in the form of degraded womanhood: 13 The woman Folly [<hi type="italic">Frau Thorheit</hi>] conducts herself boisterously,      Wantonness, and not knowing anything at all; 14 And hath seated herself at the door of her house,      On a seat high up in the city, 15 To call to those who walk in the way,      Who go straight on their path. <div eID="gen10866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10867" type="x-p"/> The connection of אשת כּסילוּת is genitival, and the genitive is not, as in אשׁת רע, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.24">Pro 6:24</reference>, specifying, but appositional, as in בת־ציון (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Isa.1.8">Isa 1:8</reference>). הומיּה [boisterous] is pred., as <reference osisRef="Prov.7.11">Pro 7:11</reference> : her object is sensual, and therefore her appearance excites passionately, overcoming the resistance of the mind by boisterousness. In 13b it is further said who and how she is. פּתיּוּת she is called as wantonness personified. This abstract פּתיּוּת, derived from פּתי, must be vocalized as אכזריּוּת; Hitzig thinks it is written with <hi type="italic">a</hi> on account of the following <hi type="italic">u</hi> sound, but this formation always ends in ijjûth, not ajjûth. But as from חזה as well חזּיון = חזיון as חזון is formed, so from פּתה as well פּתוּת like חזוּת or פּתוּת like לזוּת, רעוּת, as פּתיוּת (instead of which פּתיּוּת is preferred) can be formed; Kimchi rightly (<hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 181a) presents the word under the form פּעלוּת. With וּבל (<reference osisRef="Prov.14.7">Pro 14:7</reference>) poetic, and stronger than לאו, the designation of the subject is continued; the words וּבל־ידעה מּה (thus with <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> and without <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi> following, ידעה is to be written, after Codd. and old editions) have the value of an adjective: and not knowing anything at all (מה = τὶ, as Num 23:3; <reference osisRef="Job.13.13">Job 13:13</reference>, and here in the negative clause, as in prose מאוּמה), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, devoid of all knowledge. The Targ. translates explanatorily: not recognising טבתּא, the good; and the lxx substitutes: she knows not shame, which, according to Hitzig, supposes the word כּלמּה, approved of by him; but כלמה means always <hi type="italic">pudefactio</hi>, not <hi type="italic">pudor</hi>. To know no כלמה would be equivalent to, to let no shaming from without influence one; for shamelessness the poet would have made use of the expression ובל־ידעה בּשׁת. In וישׁבה the declaration regarding the subject beginning with הומיה is continued: Folly also has a house in which works of folly are carried one, and has set herself down by the door (לפּתח as לפי, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.3">Pro 8:3</reference>) of this house; she sits there על־כּסּא. Most interpreters here think on a throne (lxx ἐπὶ δίφρου, used especially of the <hi type="italic">sella curulis</hi>); and Zöckler, as Umbreit, Hitzig, and others, connecting genitiv. therewith מרמי קרת, changes in 14b the scene, for he removes the “high throne of the city” from the door of the house to some place elsewhere. But the sitting is in contrast to the standing and going on the part of Wisdom on the streets preaching (Evagrius well renders: <hi type="italic">in molli ignavaque sella</hi>); and if כסא and house-door are named along with each other, the former is a seat before the latter, and the accentuation rightly separates by <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi> כסא from מרמי קרת. “According to the accents and the meaning, מרמי קרת is the <hi type="italic">acc. loci</hi>: on the high places of the city, as Pro 8:2.” (Fl.). They are the high points of the city, to which, as Wisdom, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.3">Pro 9:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.2">Pro 8:2</reference>, so also Folly, her rival (wherefore <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.6">Ecc 10:6</reference> does not appertain to this place), invites followers to herself. She sits before her door to call לעברי דרך (with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, as in Cod. 1294 and old editions, without the <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>), those who go along the way (genitive connection with the supposition of the accusative construction, <hi type="italic">transire viam</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Prov.2.7">Pro 2:7</reference>), to call (invite) המישּׁרים (to be pointed with מ <hi type="italic">raphatum</hi> and <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> going before, according to Ben-Asher’s rule; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Methegsetz</hi>. §20), those who make straight their path, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, who go straight on, directly before them (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.57.2">Isa 57:2</reference>). The participial construction (the schemes <hi type="italic">amans Dei</hi> and <hi type="italic">amans Deum</hi>), as well as that of the verb קרא (first with the dat. and then with the accus.), interchange.
entries.3744f3854ef012c3f08eb05ad93df91bd2771632: <reference osisRef="Prov.9.16-Prov.9.17">Pro 9:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen10867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10868" type="x-p"/> The woman, who in her own person serves as a sign to her house, addresses those who pass by in their innocence (לתמּם, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.11">2Sa 15:11</reference>): <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.16">16</reference> “Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither!”      And if any one is devoid of understanding, she saith to him: 17 “Stolen waters taste sweet,      And the bread of secrecy is pleasant.” פּתי (folly, simplicity) has a side accessible to good and its contrary: Wisdom is connected with the one side, and Folly with the other. And as the חסר־לב offers a <hi type="italic">vacuum</hi> to Wisdom which may perhaps be filled with the right contents, so is this <hi type="italic">vacuum</hi> welcome to Folly, because it meets there no resistance. In this sense, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.16">Pro 9:16</reference> is like <reference osisRef="Prov.9.4">Pro 9:4</reference> (excepting the addition of a connecting and of a concluding ו: <hi type="italic">et si quis excors, tum dicit ei</hi>); the word is the same in both, but the meaning, according to the two speakers, is different. That to which they both invite is the pleasure of her fellowship, under the symbol of eating and drinking; in the one case it is intellectual and spiritual enjoyment, in the other sensual. That Wisdom offers (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.5">Pro 9:5</reference>) bread and wine, and Folly water and bread, has its reason in this, that the particular pleasure to which the latter invites is of a sensual kind; for to drink water out of his own or out of another fountain is (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.15-Prov.3.20">Pro 3:15-20</reference>) the symbol of intercourse in married life, or of intercourse between the unmarried, particularly of adulterous intercourse. מים גּנוּבים (correct texts have it thus, without the <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>) is sexual intercourse which is stolen from him who has a right thereto, thus carnal intercourse with אושׁת אישׁ; and לחם סתרים fleshly lust, which, because it is contrary to the law, must seek (cf. <hi type="italic">furtum</hi>, secret love intrigue) concealment (סתרים, extensive plur., as מעמקּים; Böttcher, §694). Just such pleasure, after which one wipes his mouth as if he had done nothing (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.20">Pro 30:20</reference>), is for men who are without wisdom sweet (מתק, <reference osisRef="Job.20.12">Job 20:12</reference>) and pleasant; the prohibition of it gives to such pleasure attraction, and the secrecy adds seasoning; and just such enjoyments the כסילות, personified carnality, offers. But woe to him who, befooled, enters her house!
entries.5711e854c760d54f9cfb1e7e08444d87edfd4c9b: <reference osisRef="Prov.9.18">Pro 9:18</reference> <div eID="gen10868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10869" type="x-p"/> He goes within: 18 And he knows not that the dead are there;      In the depths of Hades, her guests. <div eID="gen10869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10870" type="x-p"/> How near to one another the house of the adulteress and Hades are, so that a man passes through the one into the other, is already stated in <reference osisRef="Prov.2.18">Pro 2:18</reference>; Pro 7:27. Here, in the concluding words of the introduction to the Book of Proverbs, addressed to youth, and for the most part containing warning against sinful pleasure, these two further declarations are advanced: the company assembled in the house of lewdness consists of רפאים, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, (cf. p. 83) the old, worn-out, who are only in appearance living, who have gone down to the seeming life of the shadowy existence of the kingdom of the dead; her (כסילות) invited ones (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.7.26">Pro 7:26</reference>, her slaughtered ones) are in the depths of Hades (not in the valleys, as Umbreit, Löwenstein, and Ewald translate, but in the depths, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, ἐπὶ τοῖς βαθέσι; for עמקי is not only plur. to עמק, but also <hi type="italic">per metaplasmum</hi> to עמק, <reference osisRef="Prov.25.3">Pro 25:3</reference>, as אמרי to אמר), thus in שׁאול תּחתּית (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.22">Deu 32:22</reference>); they have forsaken the fellowship of the life and of the love of God, and have sunk into the deepest destruction. The house of infamy into which Folly allures does not only lead to hell, it is hell itself; and they who permit themselves to be thus befooled are like wandering corpses, and already on this side of death are in the realm of wrath and of the curse.<note placement="foot">The lxx has considerable additions introduced after <reference osisRef="Prov.9.18">Pro 9:18</reference>, as also after <reference osisRef="Prov.9.12">Pro 9:12</reference>, of which we shall elsewhere speak.</note>  <chapter eID="Prov.9"/> <div eID="gen10870" type="x-p"/>
